I've read plenty of commentary about the implications of the U.S. Supreme Court's recent decision in Williams-Yulee v. Florida Bar, but I haven't seen any that addresses the far scarier issue that underlies the Court's reasoning. This case was about a Florida regulation that prohibited judicial candidates from personally soliciting campaign contributions.

This post, for example, has some interesting thoughts about the Court's seeming abandonment of strict scrutiny, at least for this specific instance. But what I find most terrifying about this decision is that it relies on one basic assumption: that there is and should be a contrast between the level of trust we have in judges as the result of judicial elections and that we have in every other kind of elected official.

This isn't some great leap of logic, either; the majority says as much:

But a State’s interest in preserving public confidence in the integrity of its judiciary extends beyond its interest in preventing the appearance of corruption in legislative and executive elections. [...] Politicians are expected to be appropriately responsive to the preferences of their supporters.

Slip op. at 10-11. The Court is not talking about letters and phone calls to those politicians' offices. The last sentence there is a reference to the plurality opinion in McCutcheon v. Federal Election Comm'n, 572 U.S. _____ (2014), where the Court struck down the aggregate limit on individuals' contributions to political parties and/or campaign committees. Chief Justice Roberts, writing for the majority, then goes on to discuss how important it is that states maintain the public confidence in judicial elections, and this in turn is the state interest the Court uses to uphold the restriction on candidate speech. So what we have here is not just an assumption that non-judicial elections are inherently corrupt, but acceptance of this fact. From there, the Court concludes that judicial elections should be less so, and that this manufactured distinction can in turn be used to justify a content-based restriction on free speech. This is fruit of a most poisonous tree indeed.

Somewhat less alarming is that Justice Ginsburg wrote a concurring opinion in which she also embraces the contrast:

'Favortism and influence' are inevitable 'in representative politics.'

Slip op. at 25, quoting Citizens United v. Federal Election Comm'n, 558 U.S. 310, 359 (2010). She goes on to quote McCutcheon, just as the majority did:

"[A] central feature of democracy,” the plurality [in McCutcheon] maintained, is "that constituents support candidates who share their beliefs and interests, and candidates who are elected can be expected to be responsive to those concerns."

Id., quoting McCutcheon, 572 U.S. at ____. In context, it is absolutely clear that this is talking about campaign contributions. It's important to note that Justice Ginsburg dissented from the holdings in both McCutcheon and Citizens United, so she at least seems not to think that corruption is an inevitable part of representative politics.

In both cases, however, both Justice Ginsburg and the majority go on to cite attempts at influence peddling in judicial elections as a way to justify the Court's ultimate holding, which is again a content-based restriction on speech. So here we come to the second reason this decision is so scary, which I alluded to earlier: the Court's willingness to implement such a restriction based on corruption that a majority of jusitces has been perfectly willing to uphold in the past. Remember that all those quotes from prior cases about the "inevitability" of influence resulting from money are from cases that struck down legislative attempts to curb such corruption on, wait for it, First Amendment grounds. Meanwhile, the Court specifically declines to adopt a lesser standard of scrutiny for rules of this type, instead saying:

As we have long recognized, speech about public issues and the qualifications of candidates for elected office commands the highest level of First Amendment protection.

(Slip op. at 7). As the commentator I linked above points out, it'll likely be some time before we know just how this shakes out. But I fear that it's all too clear: the Court will continue to strike down any attempts at campaign finance reform (and will probably continue to destroy what safeguards we have), and will do so in an arbitrary way. This is little surprise of course from those of us who regularly follow legal issues, but that doesn't mean we have to like it or that we shouldn't point it out when it occurs.

I said in the title that I agree with the Court's decision, but it would be better to say that I agree with the ultimate outcome. I wholeheartedly believe in restrictions to campaign speech, and I don't think the Florida regulation goes far enough (it allows judicial candidates to find out who's donated to them so they can write thank-you notes). As this case makes quite clear, the Court is perfectly willing to pick and choose types of speech worthy of First Amendment protection, despite a previous majority's protestations to the contrary in Citizens United. But what is equally clear in light of the recent decisions in this area is that the money taps will not be turned off anytime soon without colossal changes to our existing legal framework. This too can have unintended consequences, of course, but more to the point the current state of things is such that the will is absent. Regardless, the Supreme Court has drawn one more arbitrary line where one should not be, while leaving a gaping hole a curtain wall should go.

Brief sidebar: For all the flak that it gets, Citizens United isn't quite the boogeyman that it's made out to be. It's more the continuation of a long line of bad decisions. Like most shorthand, though, it's become the stand-in for everything we don't like about money in politics but seem unwilling to do much about. This leads me to my second point, which is that all this money shouldn't matter. Really it only works because we as an electorate are content to let it. If we would stop letting ads and other vapidities guide our hands on the ballot, it would all be moot. We must remember that, in the words of a far different Court, the right to vote is the ultimate right, as it is "preservative of all rights." Yick Wo v. Hopkins, 118 U.S. 356, 370 (1886). The state can't take from us what we're unwilling to give.

I loved your post.

I can't see I agree with it %100, but here are my thoughts:

  1. Judges, as officials of the Judicial branch, serve a special function - one which requires independence by its very nature. We want adherence to the law in our judges, not political positions swayed by which individuals or organizations donated to a particular judicial campaign. I see the reasoning here. If judges are out soliciting funds- they may feel obligated to the interests of donors, not to the law. Despite all their education, and ethical obligations to the contrary, these are still people that shit the bed as children (or in the case of some of our more esteemed and elderly judges, last week). That is to say- they are simply human and subject to the same prejudices, pressures and character flaws we all are. At least this decision removes some of that temptation. I wouldn't say this speaks broadly to why courts are hesitant to deal with campaign finance reform, generally however, only as it applies to judicial elections on the state level. (Art. III judges are appointed for life...no such issue at the federal level). This case can easily be distinguished on those grounds alone. For Congressional and Presidential elections- we expect our politicians to be reactive to the populace. One of the way's we express our wishes is by donating or advocating for particular causes.

  2. As to campaign finance reform- I'm pretty libertarian, and I believe strongly in the market place of ideas.

    You can spend a billion dollars trying to pass a law that says the 2+2=5. No matter how much you spend, I think it's unlikely such a foolish idea will gain much traction in the electorate. Perhaps I put too much trust in the proles, but a certain level is required in a democracy.

    I understand the concerns- but my concerns are linked to freedom of speech and freedom of association. Each individual can spend their funds to advertise their views on the public airwaves. Free speech. Each individual may join groups which exhort the same values and petition for desired legislation. I fail to see why individuals would lose their right to spend their economic resources as they see fit, simply because they chose to do so in a group forum. It sucks when people with stupid ideas have massive amounts of money to spend, but I value the ability to publicly show the world you're an asshole more than I trust the government to tell me which type of speech related to elections is permissible.

As for your sidebar: I agree, the idea that corporations have certain rights under the law is long since established. While the decision extended those rights...I think the larger issue at play here is how willing people are to mindlessly consume media as truth without a second of hesitation or any degree of cynicism. Pass all the laws you want, you can't fix stupid.

I'm not going to address the strict scrutiny issue you brought up- simply because that whole line of jurisprudence is a poor excuse for undercutting your rights, as far as I'm concerned. ConLaw made me want to scream at anyone who would listen. No one did.

For your first point, I understand totally the impulse, and certainly agree that judges should be more above the political fray. But my concern is with we as a society taking it as an inevitable and unsolvable problem. The Supreme Court seems to be taking the stance that it's at least the former, and are in turn using this as a basis for always throwing out campaign finance laws. After all, if the laws can't solve this problem (due, at least in part, to its inherent inevitability in their minds), then they can never meet any level of scrutiny. This also runs into one of the issues I have with Libertarianism (depending on the flavor, of course): too often the definition of freedom becomes "freedom for some at the expense of others," which is absolutely what's going on here.

For your second point, I'm partially with you. As I mentioned in my original post, I too think the electorate is ultimately to blame, and I'll go so far as to say that there are limits to how much we should protect people from themselves. My issue is less with how much the rich can influence politics, but rather how little everyone else can. If you're not sponsored by one of the two major parties (who get the option of public funds, I should add), then you have to be extraordinarily wealthy to have any say at a meaningful level, at least as an individual. Sure, the less-well-off can join forces or whatever, but they'll never be able to compete with wealthy people doing the same, and more to the point they shouldn't have to. Their voices shouldn't be worth less or valued less. Now, I certainly don't think the government should be telling us, say, what kinds of ads can be run or whatever, but I don't think that's really the goal of campaign finance laws. I would much rather we adopted public funding only. I haven't worked out yet how I think we should choose who gets it, and there'll certainly have to be some minimum requirements or else we'll have 6,000 presidential candidates. But we have to try to come back from the plutocratic direction we're headed in.

I think the larger issue at play here is how willing people are to mindlessly consume media as truth without a second of hesitation or any degree of cynicism. Pass all the laws you want, you can't fix stupid.

Rant incoming.

I'd hoped to do one of those two things myself before I came out, but could never get hired (see my previous comment). One thing I will say is that you have far more potential to do justice as a prosecutor than as a defense lawyer. As a defense lawyer you spend most of your time trying to talk the prosecutor into going easy on your client (usually without any real bargaining power). Plus, as you know, the courts in general are slowly eroding constitutional protections for defendants, which means there're a lot fewer avenues there.

I didn't see too much bad behavior from other lawyers for the most part (I can only think of one truly bad one), but bear in mind most of my time has been in administrative law where the lawyers need to make me happy. I've seen plenty of incompetence, to be sure. But that's not why the profession is miserable (in both senses of the word): this series from a law professor does a far better job of digging into it.

You're right about overcrowding being part of it, but that's a symptom rather than a cause. The simple fact is that there is definitely a 1% in our profession, and they look after their own. My state's bar holds its annual meetings in a resort town, and it's mid-year meetings are always in another country. Basically, unless you have enough money to take 1-2 weeks off and go stay in Europe, they don't give a shit about you. There's plenty of little things too: you're not allowed to earn interest on your trust account (which is fair), but the Bar does; when you set it up with the bank, they do pay interest on it, it just goes to the Bar instead. Oh, and they nickle and dime you on administrative costs. But God forbid you should not pay your dues every year, even if you're unemployed. Literally the second piece of mail I got (after the letter officially telling me I was in) was a dues statement; nevermind that I hadn't had a real job in more than three years and was six figures in debt, the Bar needed to get its piece. Can't pay? Oh well, you'd better take a second job. There's no deferment for bar dues, and they start tacking on fees if you're late. When you need them they aren't there, but if you fuck up, they'll send you that "personal and confidential" letter with a quickness (thankfully I personally haven't been on a receiving end of one, but I've worked with those who have). I reached out to their support group type of thing when I was dealing with some significant depression while in private practice, and was completely ignored - I never got so much as an automated e-mail. The people that are running things in the legal profession now were generally coming through the ranks when becoming a lawyer was enough to virtually guarantee a comfortable or better standard of living, and there is a systemic failure to recognize that this is no longer the case. The cost of a JD more than doubled between the early 1990s and the mid-00s, and the pace of admissions hasn't slowed down much. The leadership (particularly in groups like the ABA) has got theirs, and they haven't shown much interest in looking out for the rest of us. It already is a race to the bottom; you look at what's happened with temp wages, and with even litigation jobs (I remember plenty of want ads offering $30-$40k in places like New York City), and the future is now. My current job (which I got in the fall of last year, so call it 5 1/2 years after admission to the bar) is the first job I've worked where I've earned more than the teachers in my county. I work a side job grading practice essays for the bar exam (the hypocrisy of which is not lost on me), and would take on another job if I had time.

Litigation ... ugh. I got a lot of grief from my trial skills professors when I said that showmanship was an important part of litigation work, but I still find their view hopelessly naïve. Jurors don't give a shit about what actually happened or what the law says. Some people enjoy this aspect of it, but I always hated it. Plus the system rewards being a pain in the ass (excuse me, "zealous representation"), and don't expect your clients to show you much if any gratitude. One of the things discussed in the link above that I absolutely found to be true was that people see us as part of their problem (or at best a necessary evil) rather than a solution to it. I spent most of my time in private practice talking my clients out of doing stupid things because they were emotional than anything, and once things were done I never talked to them again. The same is true in criminal defense only more so. I had one who had a criminal history (which he lied to me about) of doing the exact same shit he was accused of, and so we were fucked if we went to trial, as they were crimes of moral turpitude so were of course admissible if he testified. He couldn't not testify, because we had no other way to attack the prosecution's case really. When I got a deal with the prosecutor whereby he pled to a misdemeanor and stayed out of jail, he was pissed because of course he didn't do anything wrong. Nevermind that the sentencing guidelines for him were for several years, but people don't want to hear that. So don't expect anyone to be grateful for what you do.

I hope for your sake your JD was paid for already. If not, get a federal consolidation loan if you can. That I did so is literally the only reason I haven't declared bankruptcy, since they'll cap your payments based on income, and will forgive them after 10 years of doing government work (unless Congress pulls the rug out from under us). In my case, the day that happens is the last day that I'm a lawyer. The only reason I've stayed this long is because I have no other choice: I can't afford to develop any other skills, and can't make $20,000 per year even with those payment caps. But yeah, the moment I get that forgiveness letter, I'm out.

OH MY GOD THIS IS A GLORIOUS DAY!

Four years ago I was on my usual cycling route.

It was the middle of the fall, a clear skies and 70 degrees Fahrenheit.

About a mile from my house is a trail the runs by the nearby Lake.

On this particular day everything was particularly... Beautiful. It's a little hard to describe.

The trail was a mixture of green, brown, golden orange, and brilliant blue.

I rode, with the clear blue water reflecting the sky in my right. Close enough to the water that it seemed as if I was hovering past it.

To my left were the woods that the trail cut through. Brown and Vibrant Green, the trees formed a boundary between the nature of my surroundings and civilization.

Below was a flowing road of speckled red, golden orange, and soft yellow. The entire bottom of the trail, normally a pale grey, was a brilliant path of fallen leaves.

My only qualm was the trial was far too short.

I've been back to that trail dozens of times, and never again have I seen it in its total glory.

It's the most beautiful thing I've seen, and I'll never forget it.
